sections.title: The Halogens
sections.markdown:
Fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine and astatine sit together in **Group 7 of
the Periodic Table**, and the group has a name of its own: the
**[[halogen]]**s. At first sight the members look almost nothing like one
another — one is a pale gas, one a dense coloured liquid, one a shiny grey
solid — and part of this chapter is learning to see the family underneath
the differences.

Hold on to one idea from the start: the outer shell. Every Group 7 atom
carries **7 electrons in its outer shell**, and the outer shell is where
all chemistry happens. That single shared fact is why these five elements
react in similar ways, form similar compounds and show neat, predictable
trends as you descend the group — exactly the pattern you already saw for
Group 1 in Chapter 11 (u2:c11), now played out on the non-metal side of
the table.

The name *halogen* means **"salt-forming"**, and it is earned: react any
halogen with a metal and you get a **[[salt]]**. Calcium fluoride in tap
water chemistry, sodium chloride on your chips, silver bromide in
photographic film, potassium iodide in the lab — all of them are halogen
salts, and every one of them contains the same unit: the halide ion, **X⁻**
(where X stands for any halogen). One letter, one charge, one family.

Two pieces of machinery before the detail. First, the halogens are
**non-metallic** and exist as **[[diatomic]]** molecules — F₂, Cl₂, Br₂,
I₂ — two atoms bonded into one molecule, never lone atoms in the element.
Second, this chapter's evidence engine is the **displacement reaction**:
pitting one halogen against another's salt solution and watching which one
wins. Those reactions are the experimental proof that reactivity *falls*
down the group, and they are where the chapter earns its exam marks.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to state the colours and
physical states of the halogens at room temperature and explain the
physical-property trends; use the group trends to predict the properties
of halogens you have never met; carry out and interpret halogen
displacement reactions, including their ionic equations; and — for Paper 2
chemistry-only content — explain the reactivity trend in terms of
electronic configurations. Each of those builds on the last, so the order
above is the order to learn in.

:::prior-knowledge
This chapter leans on three earlier chapters. From Chapter 3 (u1:c03) you
need electronic configurations, especially the idea of outer-shell
electrons. From Chapter 4 (u1:c04) you need the Periodic Table itself —
groups as columns, and why elements in the same group share chemical
behaviour. From Chapter 8 (u1:c08) you need simple molecular structure:
diatomic molecules, covalent bonds *inside* molecules and intermolecular
forces *between* them, which power the melting-point trend in the next
section.
:::

:::exam-hint
Examiners love Group 7 because it tests whether you can *use* trends, not
just recite them. The colour-and-state table in the next section is pure
recall and appears in Paper 1C; the displacement evidence and the
electronic-configuration explanation carry the higher-value marks, and the
explanation (spec 2.8C) is chemistry-only content — Paper 2C only. If your
route is Paper 1C, nail the table, the salts and the displacement
observations; the deeper "why" can wait until you pick up the Paper 2
lane.
:::

:::misconception
"The halogens are called salt-formers, so salts are a kind of halogen."
The arrow points the other way. A **[[salt]]** is an ionic compound made
when a metal reacts with a halogen (or with an acid); the halogen is one
*reactant*, not the product category. The halogen itself is either a
reactive molecular element (Cl₂) or, inside its salts, the negative ion
X⁻ — the sodium in sodium chloride is as essential to that salt as the
chlorine is.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.5 items on colours, states and group trends. If
you can already say what "halogen" means, name the five members, give
their outer-shell electron count and write the two atoms of any halogen as
X₂, you are holding the section's load-bearing facts.
:::

sections.title: The Halogens
sections.markdown:
The atoms of fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine and astatine all have
**7 electrons in their outer shell**, and that is the whole reason they are
grouped together. The number of outer-shell electrons determines how an
atom reacts, so every Group 7 element reacts in a similar way — and the
reactions all carry the family signature: forming compounds that contain
the **X⁻ ion**, the halogen having gained one electron.

The elements themselves are non-metallic and **[[diatomic]]** — their
molecules are pairs of atoms, F₂, Cl₂, Br₂, I₂. Memorise the physical
profile the family walks through as the molecules get heavier:

| Halogen | Formula | Physical state at room temperature | Colour |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fluorine | F₂ | gas | yellow |
| Chlorine | Cl₂ | gas | green |
| Bromine | Br₂ | liquid | red-brown liquid, orange/brown vapour |
| Iodine | I₂ | solid | grey solid, purple vapour |

Read the table as a trend, not a list. Down the group the melting points
and boiling points **increase** — gas → liquid → solid — and the colour
becomes **darker**. Both trends have one cause. The halogens are all
covalent molecular substances, and as the relative molecular mass
increases down the group the **[[intermolecular-forces]]** of attraction
between molecules become stronger, so more energy is needed to overcome
them. That is what melting and boiling actually are: separating molecules
from each other, not breaking the covalent bonds inside them. No covalent
bond is broken when iodine melts — the I–I bonds within each I₂ molecule
survive intact.

Being non-metals, the halogens are poor conductors of heat and
electricity, in both their solid and liquid states — there are no
delocalised electrons to carry charge, unlike the metallic bonding of
Chapter 9 (u1:c09).

One member needs special handling: **astatine**. It is radioactive,
formed during the radioactive decay of other elements such as uranium and
thorium, and most of its isotopes are so unstable that a sample decays
away almost as fast as it forms — which is why no one has ever assembled
a visible quantity of it. Everything you can say about astatine in an
exam is a *prediction* from the group trend, which is exactly what the
closing section of this chapter trains you to do.

:::key-point
Hydrogen chloride the gas and hydrochloric acid the solution are **two
different substances**. Hydrogen chloride is a gas of covalent HCl
molecules; hydrochloric acid is a solution containing H⁺ and Cl⁻ ions.
The other [[hydrogen-halide]]s follow the same pattern when dissolved:
HF(aq) is hydrofluoric acid, HBr(aq) is hydrobromic acid, HI(aq) is
hydroiodic acid. Gas = molecules; solution = ions.
:::

:::exam-hint
The melting-point explanation is a three-mark skeleton, and the mark
scheme pays each bone separately: (1) the intermolecular forces of
attraction get **stronger** down the group as the relative molecular mass
increases; (2) therefore **more energy** is needed to overcome them;
(3) the covalent bonds within the molecules are **not** broken. Answers
that say "bigger atoms have stronger bonds" score zero — the bonds being
overcome are *between* molecules, not inside them.
:::

:::misconception
"Iodine must have strong covalent bonds, because it is a solid at room
temperature." Swap the word *covalent* for *intermolecular* and the
sentence becomes correct. Iodine is a solid because its molecules attract
each other strongly enough that room temperature cannot pull the lattice
apart — but those I₂ molecules are held together inside by ordinary
covalent bonds, and those bonds never break on melting or boiling. State
changes in molecular substances are a story about **[[intermolecular-forces]]**,
never about the covalent bonds themselves.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.5 items on the physical-state table and the
melting/boiling-point trend. Test yourself now: which halogens are gases
at room temperature? Why does bromine melt at a higher temperature than
chlorine? What is the difference between hydrogen chloride gas and
hydrochloric acid? Three right answers and this section is banked.
:::

sections.title: Safety
sections.markdown:
Before any halogen reaction, the hazards — because this family is the
most dangerous set of elements you will meet. **Fluorine**
is so dangerously reactive that you would never expect to find it in a
school lab at all; the reactions it drives are violent beyond anything a
teaching room is equipped to control. The school-taught members —
chlorine, bromine, iodine — are manageable, but only inside a
discipline: **all the halogens have extremely poisonous vapours**, so
every experiment with them is carried out in a **[[fume-cupboard]]**,
which pulls the toxic vapours away from the air you breathe.

Liquid **bromine** adds a second hazard: it is **very corrosive**, and
great care is taken to keep it off the skin. A drop of bromine on bare
skin burns chemically — that is what corrosive means — so bromine
handling is gloves, goggles and a fume cupboard, every time. Chlorine is
a gas with a choking, poisonous vapour; iodine is the gentlest of the
three but still stains and irritates, and its vapour is not something to
breathe by choice.

The safety picture is itself part of the chemistry. The same high
reactivity that makes halogens superb salt-formers makes their vapours
destructive to living tissue, and reactivity (like the boiling points)
tracks the group trend — fluorine at the top is the worst of the family,
which is precisely why it has no place in a school lab.

:::safety
Fluorine is far too dangerously reactive for school use — expect never to
see it in a teaching lab. Apart from the reactivity of the elements
(especially fluorine and chlorine), **all halogen vapours are extremely
poisonous**: halogen work belongs in a fume cupboard. **Liquid bromine is
very corrosive** — keep it off the skin, wear eye protection and gloves,
and treat any spill as a stop-work event.
:::

:::exam-hint
Hazard questions are free marks if you use the right register. The mark
scheme wants the formal hazard words — **toxic** (poisonous vapours),
**corrosive** (bromine attacks skin) — paired with the matching control
measure: experiments in a fume cupboard because the vapours are poisonous.
Writing "dangerous" or "not nice" earns nothing; writing "chlorine has a
toxic vapour, so the experiment is carried out in a fume cupboard" earns
both marks every time.
:::

:::misconception
"Chlorine can't be that dangerous — swimming pools use it." The chemical
in the pool is not the element; it is a vanishingly dilute solution of
chlorine compounds that kill bacteria at parts per million. The element
chlorine is a toxic green gas that attacked soldiers in the First World
War. Same family, utterly different scales — and the dilution is exactly
the point: hazards live with concentration, not with the name of the
element.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.5 items that pair halogen properties with lab
handling. Can you name the one halogen that never appears in school labs,
the reason all halogen work happens in a fume cupboard, and the extra
hazard liquid bromine carries on top of its vapour? Those three answers
are the whole section.
:::

sections.title: Reactions of the Halogens
sections.markdown:
Two reaction families carry the halogens' chemistry, and both are
formula-patterns you can write for any member of the group. Learn the
pattern once, and every individual equation is a substitution exercise.

**Reaction 1: with hydrogen.** Every halogen combines with hydrogen to
form a **[[hydrogen-halide]]**, HX — hydrogen fluoride, hydrogen chloride,
hydrogen bromide, hydrogen iodide:

H₂(g) + Br₂(g) → 2HBr(g)

The hydrogen halides are all **acidic, poisonous gases**. In common with
every compound formed between two non-metals, they are covalent molecular
substances — and, like all acids, they dissolve in water to give acidic
solutions. Hydrochloric acid *is* hydrogen chloride dissolved in water;
the same gas-to-acid story gives hydrofluoric, hydrobromic and hydroiodic
acids. The gas and the solution are different substances with different
structures (molecules in the gas, ions in the solution) — the distinction
the previous section's key point pinned down.

**Reaction 2: with metals.** React a halogen with a metal and you form an
ionic **[[salt]]**. Sodium burning in chlorine is the demonstration to
picture: it burns with its typical yellow flame and the product is white,
solid sodium chloride,

2Na(s) + Cl₂(g) → 2NaCl(s)

an ionic solid built from Na⁺ and Cl⁻. The pattern generalises across the
Group 1 and Group 2 metals: when halogens react with these metals, the
metal atoms lose electrons and the halogen atoms gain them, so the
products are ionic — M⁺ and X⁻ packed into a lattice. With non-metals,
by contrast, halogens form covalent molecular compounds (the hydrogen
halides are the standing example). Metal + halogen = ionic; non-metal +
halogen = molecular. That single sentence sorts every halogen product on
the course.

One caution about scope. Most of the group chemistry you meet — the
reactions above, the displacement work coming next — is taught through
the three commonly used halogens, chlorine, bromine and iodine. The
patterns do not stop there: the trend runs on through the rest of the
group, which is what lets you make confident statements about fluorine
above them and astatine below them. Fluorine's extra violence is real but
unprintable in a school context; astatine's behaviour is invisible but
predictable. The three lab halogens are the family's public face.

:::key-point
Chlorine, bromine and iodine are the three commonly used halogens of
school chemistry — but the trends continue for the **rest of the group**.
Reactivity keeps rising towards fluorine and keeps falling towards
astatine; every family pattern you meet in this chapter transfers to the
members you never see.
:::

:::exam-hint
Equation marks live in the details: state symbols and balancing. The
hydrogen halides form from gaseous hydrogen and gaseous halogen
(H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2HCl(g)), and sodium's reaction needs the 2:2:2
balancing (2Na(s) + Cl₂(g) → 2NaCl(s)) because chlorine is a **diatomic**
molecule — one Cl₂ delivers two chloride ions. Candidates who write
Na + Cl₂ → NaCl lose the balancing mark on every version of this
question; the diatomic habit is worth practising until it is automatic.
:::

:::misconception
"Hydrochloric acid must be an ionic compound, because acids contain
H⁺ ions." The ions appear only in *solution*. Dry hydrogen chloride gas
is a simple molecular substance — covalent H–Cl molecules, no ions, no
conduction. Dissolve it in water and the molecules react with the water
to form H⁺(aq) and Cl⁻(aq). The acid behaviour belongs to the solution;
the compound in the gas state is molecular like every other non-metal +
non-metal product.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.6 items on halogen reaction patterns and their
prediction use. Write the equation for hydrogen burning in chlorine, name
the acid its product forms in water, and give the formula of the salt
made when potassium burns in bromine. If those took you under a minute,
the reaction families are yours.
:::

sections.title: Reacting Chlorine with Potassium Bromide or Potassium Iodide Solutions
sections.markdown:
Put a more reactive halogen into a solution of a less reactive halogen's
salt and the newcomer takes over: it pushes the original halogen out of
solution and takes its place. These are **[[displacement-reaction]]**s,
and they are the experimental engine of this chapter — a way of *ranking*
the halogens by reactivity using nothing more than colour changes.

**Demo 1: chlorine water + potassium bromide solution.** Add orange-free
— colourless — potassium bromide solution to chlorine water and the
mixture turns **orange**: bromine has been formed.

Cl₂(aq) + 2KBr(aq) → 2KCl(aq) + Br₂(aq)

Chlorine is more reactive than bromine, and it has **displaced** the
bromine from solution. The way to think about it: a more reactive element
has a greater tendency to react and form a compound; a less reactive
element is more likely to fall back to being the free, unreacted element.
Chlorine wins the compound-forming contest, so bromine is pushed back out
as the element.

**Demo 2: chlorine water + potassium iodide solution.** The same
experiment with potassium iodide solution gives a **brown** solution
(orange if very dilute) — iodine has been displaced:

Cl₂(aq) + 2KI(aq) → 2KCl(aq) + I₂(aq)

And the ladder keeps its order one rung down: bromine water added to
potassium iodide solution also gives brown iodine,

Br₂(aq) + 2KI(aq) → 2KBr(aq) + I₂(aq)

because bromine, though weaker than chlorine, is still stronger than
iodine. Reactivity falls down the group, and every one of these
colour changes is a measurement of that fall.

Colour is your observation data in these experiments, so the shades need
to be exact. Pure liquid bromine is red-brown — but **bromine in solution
is orange**, and a very dilute solution can look yellow. Iodine in
solution is brown (yellow-brown when dilute). Learn the in-solution
colours, not the neat-element colours, because exams show you solutions.

:::key-point
Colour discipline for displacement work: pure liquid bromine is
**red-brown**, bromine **in solution** is **orange** (dilute: yellow);
iodine in solution is **brown** (dilute: yellow-brown). Observations
should name the solution colour, and the displaced halogen, every time.
:::

:::exam-hint
Precision of wording is marked directly: write **"chlorine displaces
bromine"**, never "chlorine displaces bromide". Bromine is the displaced
*element* (Br₂); bromide is the *ion* (Br⁻) that sat in the salt before
the reaction. The same grammar fixes every variant: "bromine displaces
iodine", "chlorine displaces iodine". An answer that swaps element and
ion names reads as if the chemistry itself is muddled — and the mark
scheme treats it that way.
:::

:::misconception
"The solution turned orange because potassium bromide solution is orange."
Potassium bromide solution is **colourless** — the orange appears only
*because* bromine is produced by the reaction. In every displacement
observation, the colour you see belongs to the **displaced halogen**
formed as a product, never to the salt that was already there. Read the
colour, name the displaced halogen: orange → bromine; brown → iodine.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.7 items on displacement evidence for the Group
7 reactivity trend. State what you would observe when chlorine water is
added to potassium iodide solution, write the equation, and explain why
adding iodine solution to potassium bromide solution produces no change.
That trio *is* the displacement experiment in exam form.
:::

sections.title: Displacement Reactions Involving the Halogens
sections.markdown:
The demos in the previous section generalise into a rule, and the rule
has three parts. **First, the rule itself:** a more reactive halogen
displaces a less reactive halogen from its salt solution — and the
reverse never happens. Test the impossible directions and nothing occurs:

- bromine + potassium chloride solution: **no reaction** — the less
  reactive bromine cannot displace the more reactive chlorine;
- iodine + potassium chloride solution: **no reaction**;
- iodine + potassium bromide solution: **no reaction**.

Every "no visible change" here is as informative as a colour change: the
displacement ladder Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂ is confirmed by the reactions that
*fail* as much as by the ones that work.

**Second, what the metal ion is doing: nothing.** Remember that when an
ionic compound dissolves in water, it splits into its ions. So potassium
bromide solution is really a soup of K⁺(aq) and Br⁻(aq) ions, and when
chlorine reacts with it, the chlorine attacks the **bromide ion** — the
potassium ion never changes. It would make no difference if we used sodium
bromide or magnesium bromide instead: the reaction happens between the
chlorine molecule and the bromide ion, and the metal ion is a
**[[spectator-ion]]**. Write the chlorine + potassium iodide reaction
showing every charge and you can see it:

2K⁺(aq) + 2I⁻(aq) + Cl₂(aq) → 2K⁺(aq) + 2Cl⁻(aq) + I₂(aq)

The K⁺ ions stand identical on both sides — untouched. Delete them and
you get the equation that matters, the **[[ionic-equation]]**:

Cl₂(aq) + 2I⁻(aq) → 2Cl⁻(aq) + I₂(aq)

Same surgery on the bromide reaction gives:

Cl₂(aq) + 2Br⁻(aq) → 2Cl⁻(aq) + Br₂(aq)

and for bromine against iodide:

Br₂(aq) + 2I⁻(aq) → 2Br⁻(aq) + I₂(aq)

**Third, these are redox reactions.** Remind yourself of the two
definitions: **oxidation is loss of electrons, reduction is gain**. In the
chlorine + bromide reaction the chlorine takes electrons *away from* the
bromide ions — so it **oxidises** them, while the Cl₂ molecules **gain**
electrons and are reduced to Cl⁻. The electron-thief is called an
**[[oxidising-agent]]**: it oxidises something else by taking its
electrons, and because it accepts those electrons it is itself reduced.
The robbed party — the bromide ion, which gave electrons away and was
oxidised — played the matching role of **[[reducing-agent]]**. Every
halogen displacement reaction is a [[redox-reaction]] with the halogen
molecule as oxidising agent and the halide ion as reducing agent, and the
oxidising strength runs down the group exactly as reactivity does:
chlorine is a stronger oxidising agent than bromine, which is stronger
than iodine. Chlorine can oxidise bromide *and* iodide ions; bromine can
oxidise iodide ions but not chloride ions; iodine can oxidise neither.

One asymmetry to carry carefully: this "most reactive = strongest
oxidising agent" logic works for **non-metals only**. For metals the
ordering flips purpose — the most reactive metal is the best *reducing*
agent. The difference traces to the ions each family forms: non-metals
react to form negative ions (they take electrons), metals react to form
positive ions (they give them away).

And fluorine gets one honest footnote. The trend explanation coming in the
next section would predict, correctly, that fluorine out-reacts chlorine
— but the true microscopic reason does *not* fit the family pattern:
fluorine atoms do not actually accept electrons more easily than chlorine
atoms do. Its exceptional violence traces to the unusually weak bond
between the F₂ atoms. At International GCSE you will not be asked to
explain why fluorine beats chlorine; the standard group-trend argument is
the accepted answer at this level if the question ever appears.

:::exam-hint
Ionic equations are the mark-scheme's favourite way to test whether you
understand displacement or merely watched it. The recipe: write the full
equation with all ions and state symbols, strike out the spectators that
appear unchanged on both sides, keep the rest balanced and charged —
charges must balance too (2− on the left as 2I⁻, 2− on the right as 2Cl⁻).
"Cl₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + I₂" with state symbols and balanced charges is a
full-credit answer; including K⁺ is not — it signals you have not found
the [[spectator-ion]].
:::

:::misconception
"In chlorine + potassium bromide, the potassium is displaced because it
is the less reactive partner." Nothing happens to the potassium at all.
Displacement is a contest **between halogens**: the chlorine molecule
takes electrons from **bromide ions**, and the K⁺ ions drift through the
solution unchanged on both sides. The metal ion is the stage, not a
performer — that is precisely why the ionic equation can leave it out
without losing any chemistry.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.7 items on displacement, ionic equations and
the oxidising-strength ladder. Write the ionic equation for bromine water
reacting with potassium iodide solution, name the oxidising and reducing
agents in it, and predict whether iodine solution will oxidise chloride
ions. Three for three means the redox view of Group 7 is in place.
:::

sections.title: Explaining the Trend in the Reactivity of the Halogens
sections.markdown:
Here is the Paper-2 crown of the chapter: *why* does reactivity fall down
Group 7? The answer runs through how a halogen reacts. In the reactions of
this chapter, a halogen reacts by **forming a 1− ion** — it takes
electrons away from something else (a metal atom, or a [[halide-ion]] in
solution). So reactivity measures how eagerly the atom can *gain* an
electron, and that eagerness depends on one geometric fact: the size of
the atom.

A chlorine atom is **smaller** than a bromine atom. Add an electron to
each and the chlorine's new electron enters a shell **closer to the
nucleus** — chlorine has fewer filled shells in the way. An electron in a
shell closer to the nucleus is **more strongly attracted** to it. So
chlorine pulls the incoming electron in more strongly, forms its 1− ion
more readily, and therefore has the stronger tendency to react: chlorine
out-reacts bromine, and will take an electron away from a bromide ion.
Down the group the atoms grow shell by shell, the incoming electron sits
further from the nucleus, the attraction weakens, electron-gaining gets
harder — and reactivity falls: Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂.

This is the mirror image of the Group 1 story from Chapter 11 (u2:c11).
There, reactivity *rose* down the group because losing an electron gets
*easier* as the outer electron sits further out. Here, reactivity *falls*
down the group because gaining one gets *harder*. Same physics —
outer-shell distance controls electrostatics — opposite directions,
because the families do opposite jobs with the electron.

:::exam-hint
The explanation question (spec 2.8C, Paper 2 only) pays out in a fixed
chain — write all four links: (1) halogens react by **gaining one
electron** to form a 1− ion; (2) down the group the atoms get **bigger**,
so the new electron enters a shell **further from the nucleus**; (3) the
attraction it feels is **weaker**; (4) so the atom gains the electron
**less readily** — reactivity decreases. Answers that skip link 1 (how
halogens react) or that write only "bigger atoms are less reactive" drop
half the marks: the mark scheme wants the mechanism, not the slogan.
:::

:::misconception
"Bromine should attract a new electron more strongly than chlorine — its
nucleus has 35 protons against chlorine's 17." The proton count is not
what the incoming electron feels. The inner, filled shells shield it:
chlorine's 17 protons minus 10 inner-shell electrons leave the newcomer
feeling a net pull of **7+**, and bromine's 35 protons minus 28 inner
electrons leave it feeling the **same 7+**. With equal pull, the contest
is decided by **distance** — and chlorine's incoming electron starts
closer, so it wins. (This shielding argument is extension territory: the
required-at-IG explanation is the size-and-distance chain above.)
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.8C items on the electronic-configuration
explanation. Without looking back, deliver the four-link chain: how a
halogen reacts, what happens to atomic size down the group, what that
does to the attraction on the incoming electron, and what that does to
reactivity. If the chain comes out in order and in full sentences, the
hardest marks in this chapter are yours.
:::

sections.title: Summarising the Main Features of the Group Elements
sections.markdown:
Everything the chapter taught, compressed onto one card. The Group 7
elements:

- have **[[diatomic]]** molecules, X₂ (F₂, Cl₂, Br₂, I₂);
- go from **gas to liquid to solid** as you descend the group — melting
  points and boiling points increase;
- have **coloured, poisonous vapours** — the colours darken down the
  group;
- form compounds of formula **HX** with hydrogen (HF, HCl, HBr, HI),
  which dissolve in water to form **acids**;
- form **ionic [[salt]]s with metals** and **covalent compounds with
  non-metals**;
- form **X⁻ ions** (F⁻, Cl⁻, Br⁻) in their ionic compounds;
- become **less reactive** towards the bottom of the group;
- **displace elements lower down** the group from their salts.

Each line is a lever for prediction, and prediction is the last skill
this chapter hands you. Take **astatine** — the element below iodine, so
rare and radioactive that no one has ever seen a sample of it. You have
never observed astatine, and you do not need to: every property above
extrapolates down one more rung. Astatine will be:

- a **darker colour than iodine** — very dark grey or black;
- a **solid** at room temperature, with a **higher melting point** than
  iodine's;
- **diatomic**, existing as At₂ molecules;
- reactive with hydrogen to form **HAt**, which dissolves in water to
  form an **acid**;
- a salt-former with metals — **NaAt** with sodium, **KAt** with
  potassium;
- built around the **astatide ion, At⁻**, in its ionic salts;
- **less reactive than iodine**;
- **displaced from solution by iodine**.

Notice what happened there: eight properties, zero experiments. The
trend in physical properties predicted the state, the colour, the
melting point; the reaction families predicted the formulas (HAt, NaAt,
KAt, At⁻); the displacement ladder predicted who beats whom in solution.
That is the real power of a chemical family — knowledge of a few members
plus the trend is knowledge of all of them, and this exact move (trend +
application) is what prediction questions on Paper 2 are built from.

:::summary
Group 7 in one breath: **diatomic, coloured, poisonous non-metals** that
go gas → liquid → solid and darker down the group; strong intermolecular
forces make melting and boiling points rise (no covalent bonds break);
they form HX acids with hydrogen, ionic salts with metals, covalent
molecules with non-metals, always carrying X⁻ in salts; reactivity
**falls** down the group because the incoming electron lands further from
the nucleus — so any halogen displaces the halogens below it from their
salt solutions, and astatine below iodine is blacker, more solid, less
reactive, and beatable by everything above it.
:::

:::cross-curricular
The halogens work far outside the lab. Chlorine's poisonous reactivity is
put to work in water treatment, where trace chlorine kills bacteria in
drinking water and swimming pools — dilution flips the hazard. Fluoride
compounds strengthen tooth enamel against decay. Silver bromide's
light-sensitivity underpinned photographic film for over a century. And
the family's readiness to form salts explains why iodide is added to
table salt in many countries to prevent thyroid disease.
:::

:::exam-hint
Prediction questions are template questions. The formula: **state the
trend, then apply it with a comparison word**. "Astatine will be less
reactive than iodine because reactivity decreases down Group 7" — trend
named, direction named, comparison explicit — is full marks. Answers
that predict correctly but never cite the trend ("it will be a black
solid") collect the property mark and drop the reasoning mark. And in
displacement predictions, remember who displaces whom: astatine is
displaced *by* iodine, never the reverse.
:::

:::misconception
"Astatine's properties are unknowable — no one has ever seen it." The
elements below iodine in the group were all *predicted* before they were
ever isolated, for exactly the reason this chapter works: group position
plus measured trends fix the properties. Astatine's state, colour,
melting point, molecular formula, salt formulas and reactivity all follow
from lines you can already recite. "Never seen a sample" is a statement
about rarity and radioactivity, not about knowledge.
:::
